abstract: Third report in OpenAI Economic Research's 'Work at the Frontier' series, written with Upwork and published November 10, 2026 (cited as Chin, Kala, Kunievsky, Liu, Richmond and Shan, 'The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age'). It compares a sample of over 36,000 ChatGPT conversations against Upwork Marketplace job postings to ask what clients now hire freelancers to do, and what they pay for it. The central finding is about scope rather than price: AI-related postings carry fixed-price budgets about 52 percent higher after adjustment and about 41 percent more hours per hired hourly contract, while the adjusted gap in posted hourly rates is roughly 1.5 percent. The authors read this as rebundling - AI-related work combining more and less familiar tasks into larger projects - rather than as a wage premium for AI skills.
keyFindings: Posted fixed-price budgets are approximately 70 percent higher for AI-related postings than for non-AI work, and about 52 percent higher after controlling for work subcategory and posting month.
The gap in posted hourly rates is far smaller: about 9 percent raw, falling to roughly 1.5 percent after the same adjustment. The authors describe this adjusted gap as negligible.

Among hired hourly contracts with positive recorded hours, hours worked in the first 90 days after hire are approximately 41 percent higher for AI-related work. Taken with the budget and rate figures, this points to larger projects rather than a higher price for an identical unit of labour.

Of 63 matched work subcategories, 43 (68.3 percent) follow the substitution-consistent pattern - lower ChatGPT intensity with gains in Upwork share, or higher intensity with losses. 6 (9.5 percent) combined higher ChatGPT intensity with share gains and 14 (22.2 percent) combined lower intensity with losses, which is why the authors conclude 'There is not a simple substitution pattern.'

Activity mixes differ sharply between the two platforms. Content writing and professional and business writing are 14.5 percent and 10.2 percent of sampled ChatGPT conversations against roughly 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent of Upwork job posts, while graphic and presentation design, video and animation, quality-assurance testing, mobile development, digital marketing and web development are substantially larger shares of Upwork postings than of ChatGPT use.

Within AI-related postings the task mix broadened between early 2023 and late 2025, from an effective 14.6 to 21.2 equally common task clusters, about 45 percent more diverse. Video production, social-media campaign management, marketing automation and AI API integration gained share; AI-generated written content, training programs, cloud infrastructure and several writing and data activities lost share. The largest cluster, building chatbots and machine-learning models, fell from 21.8 percent to 17.8 percent.

AI-related postings more often combine task pairs that rarely appeared together before: historically uncommon pairs are 8.4 percent of within-posting pairs in AI-related jobs against 2.4 percent in other jobs, and AI-related jobs account for 54 percent of appearances of historically uncommon pairs against 13 percent for established pairs.

Context the report cites for scale: Upwork's 2026 Future Workforce Index finds 38 percent of skilled US knowledge workers freelance, and its prior annual study estimated 1.5 trillion dollars in US freelance knowledge-work earnings in 2024.
methodology: Two linked datasets. ChatGPT shares come from over 36,000 sampled personal and work-related conversations classified into the Upwork taxonomy by a privacy-preserving classifier, with schoolwork, unclear-purpose and unmatched conversations excluded; ChatGPT shares cover January 2025 to June 2026 in the public summary and H2 2025 in the AI-intensity construction. Upwork shares are Marketplace job posts, H1 2026 for levels and H1 2025 to H1 2026 for share changes, with H1 2023 as the baseline for the AI-intensity comparison. Price and hours comparisons use Upwork data through April 2026; adjusted estimates control for work subcategory and posting month, report 95 percent confidence intervals, and trim the top 1 percent of posted prices. AI-related postings are those requesting AI skills, requiring AI tools, or involving improvement of AI-generated output, classified at the level of the whole posting rather than the individual task.
qualifiers: Every price figure is a cross-sectional gap between AI-related and non-AI postings at a point in time, not a change in freelancer rates over time, which is why they sit on freelancer-rate-impact as directional signals rather than as data points in that graph's unit. Posted budgets and rates are what clients advertise, not what freelancers are ultimately paid; only the hours measure is realised. One marketplace is not the freelance economy, and Upwork's composition differs from freelance work generally. The AI-related classification applies to a whole posting, so a posting counted as AI-related may contain mostly non-AI tasks. The task-diversity and posting-mix findings run through late 2025 while prices run through April 2026, so the two halves of the report describe partly different windows. OpenAI is a party to the subject matter, and the report is co-authored with the marketplace supplying the data; it is treated as Tier 2 industry research accordingly. The writing figures and the visual-production figures point in opposite directions for creative work - writing is where direct ChatGPT use concentrates and where freelance share is thinnest - so the source should not be read as uniformly good or bad news for creative roles.
